title: The Northern Lights Could Be Visible in 12 States Tonight—Here's What to Know
excerpt: Watch the auroras light up the night sky.
content:
Your holiday light display might get a run for its money tonight, as the northern lights are expected to appear across parts of the northern U.S.

A strong stream of solar wind is predicted to interact with Earth's magnetic field, triggering auroras overnight Tuesday, November 17, into Wednesday morning.

According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), a G1 geomagnetic storm is expected, which could make auroras visible in the northern states near the Canadian border.

The Kp index is expected to reach 4.67 overnight. The Kp index is a numeric scale, ranging from zero to nine, that describes geomagnetic activity. A Kp index in the 3 to 5 range means the auroras may become brighter and activity will increase. Also, the higher the number, the farther south the northern lights may appear.

If G1 conditions develop, parts of the northern U.S., including Alaska, Idaho, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin, will have the greatest chance of experiencing the northern lights, according to the SWPC's current aurora forecast.

If you're in the northern U.S. and want to catch the display, head outside between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. local time and find a north-facing spot with a clear view of the horizon, far from light pollution. Be sure to give your eyes time to adjust, and use your phone's camera to scan the sky, as it's better at picking up faint auroras than the naked eye.

Keep in mind that tonight's first-quarter moon will be about 50 percent illuminated, which may interfere with spotting fainter auroras.
